00035ad0 Fill the output tensor with int32 samples from uniform distribution [`min`, `max`].
00035b25 - The range can be defined either by arguments or input blobs. `min` and `max` are inclusive.
00035b83     - If the range is given by input blobs, you also need to give the shape as input.
00035bd9     - When the range is given as arguments, this operator enforces min <= max. When the range is given as inputs, the constraint is not enforced.
00035c6b     - When the range is given as inputs and max < min, the first dimension of the output is set to 0. This behavior is allowed so that dynamically sampling indices into a dynamically sized tensor is possible.
00035d3c - The shape of the output can be given as argument or input.

00036bf4 The transposed convolution consumes an input vector, the filter blob, and
00036c3e the bias blob, and computes the output. Note that other parameters, such as
00036c8a the stride and kernel size, or the pads' sizes in each direction are not
00036cd3 necessary for input because they are provided by the
00036d08 ConvTransposeUnpoolOpBase operator. Various dimension checks are done
00036d4e implicitly, and the sizes are specified in the Input docs for this operator.
00036d9b As is expected, the filter is deconvolved with a subset of the
00036dda image and the bias is added; this is done throughout the image data and the
00036e26 output is computed. As a side note on the implementation layout:
00036e67 conv_transpose_op_impl.h is the templated implementation of the
00036ea7 conv_transpose_op.h file, which is why they are separate files.
00036eeb PadImage pads values around the boundary of an image according to the pad
00036f35 values and stride sizes defined by the ConvPoolOpBase operator.
00036f79 The ConvTranspose op takes an input data tensor $X$, an input weight tensor $filter$, and optionally an input bias tensor $bias$. It then computes the transposed convolution, sometimes referred to as deconvolution, and produces a single output tensor $Y$. The hyperparameters of the op such as kernel size, stride, and padding are specified as args. At each stride, the filter is deconvolved with a subset of $X$ and the $bias$ is added. This is done throughout the input data until the output computation is complete.
00037181 The output shapes are computed as follows. The number of channels in the output feature map is the number of kernels specified in the filter blob. The spatial height and width are computed as:
00037243 $$H_{out} = (H_{in}-1)*strides[0] - 2*pads[0] + kernels[0]$$
00037282 $$W_{out} = (W_{in}-1)*strides[1] - 2*pads[1] + kernels[1]$$
000372c0 Note on the implementation layout: conv_transpose_op_impl.h is the templated implementation of the conv_transpose_op.h file, which is why they are separate files. Also, in the implementation this operator inherits from the *ConvTransposeUnpoolOpBase* operator.
000373c6 Github Links:
000373d4 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/main/caffe2/operators/conv_transpose_op.h
00037428 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/main/caffe2/operators/conv_transpose_op.cc
0003747d - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/main/caffe2/operators/conv_transpose_unpool_op_base.h

0003a5be Applies spatial batch normalization to the input tensor as described in the original paper, [Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167). Be aware, this operator has two different output sets, depending on the value of *is_test*. According to the paper, the primary operation of spatial batch normalization is:
0003a74a $$Y = \frac{X - \mu_x}{\sqrt{\sigma^2_{x} + \epsilon}}*\gamma + b$$
0003a78f In the equation, $\mu_x$ is the *mean*, $X$ is the input data, $\sigma^2_{x}$ is the *var*, $\epsilon$ is *epsilon*, $\gamma$ is the *scale*, $b$ is the *bias*, and $Y$ is the output data. The *momentum* arg also affects this calculation in the computation of the running mean and variance. The influence of *momentum* is as follows:
0003a8de $$running\_mean = running\_mean * momentum + mean * (1 - momentum)$$
0003a924 $$running\_var = running\_var * momentum + var * (1 - momentum)$$
0003a967 Output when is_test = 0 (train mode): *Y, mean, var, saved_mean, saved_var*
0003a9b4 Output when is_test = 1 (test mode): *Y*
0003a9de Github Links:
0003a9ec - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/caffe2/operators/spatial_batch_norm_op.cc

0003d57e The *InstanceNorm* op applies Instance Normalization over a 4D input as described in [Instance Normalization: The Missing Ingredient for Fast Stylization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.08022).
0003d63d $$output = \frac{input-\mu_{input}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{input}^2} + \epsilon}*scale + bias$$
0003d695 Notice, two of the outputs are optional so there are three output cases for this op. Case 1: output; Case 2: output, saved_mean; Case 3: output, saved_mean, saved_inv_stdev.

0003e4ca Fill the output tensor with float samples from uniform distribution [`min`, `max`].
0003e51f - The range can be defined either by arguments or input blobs. `min` and `max` are inclusive.
0003e57d     - If the range is given by input blobs, you also need to give the shape as input.
0003e5d3     - When the range is given as arguments, this operator enforces min <= max. When the range is given as inputs, the constraint is not enforced.
0003e665     - When the range is given as inputs and max < min, the first dimension of the output is set to 0. This behavior is allowed so that dynamically sampling indices into a dynamically sized tensor is possible.
0003e736 - The shape of the output can be given as argument or input.
0003e774 Github Links:

0003f5fe The FC operator computes an output $(Y)$ as a linear combination of the input data blob $(X)$ with a weight blob $(W)$ and bias blob $(b)$. More formally,
0003f69a $$Y = XW^T+b$$
0003f6aa Here, $X$ is a matrix of shape $(M,K)$, $W$ is a matrix of shape $(N,K)$, $b$ is a vector of length $N$, and $Y$ is a matrix of shape $(M,N)$. $N$ can be thought of as the number of nodes in the layer, $M$ is the batch size, and $K$ is the number of features in an input observation.
0003f7c7 *NOTE: $X$ does not need to explicitly be a 2-dimensional matrix, however, if it is not it will be coerced into one. For an arbitrary $n$-dimensional tensor $X$, e.g. $[a_0, a_1, \ldots ,a_{k-1}, a_k, \ldots , a_{n-1}]$, where $a_i$ in $N$, and $k$ is the $axis$ arg provided, then $X$ will be coerced into a 2-dimensional tensor with dimensions $[a_0 * \ldots * a_{k-1}, a_k * \ldots * a_{n-1}]$. For the default case where axis=1, this means the $X$ tensor will be coerced into a 2D tensor of dimensions $[a_0, a_1 * \ldots * a_{n-1}]$, where $a_0$ is often the batch size. In this situation, we must have $a_0 = M$ and $a_1 * \ldots * a_{n-1} = K$. Lastly, even though $b$ is a vector of length $N$, it is copied and resized to shape $(M x N)$ implicitly, then added to each vector in the batch.*
0003fae8 Github Links:
0003faf6 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/caffe2/operators/fully_connected_op.h
0003fb4b - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/caffe2/operators/fully_connected_op.cc
0003fba2 <details>
0003fbad <summary> <b>Example</b> </summary>
0003fbd2 **Code**
0003fbe1 // In this example, our batch size is 1 (M=1), the input observation will have
0003fc30 //   6 features (K=6), and the layer will have one hidden node (N=1). The
0003fc7a //   expected output is Y=7.
0003fc97 workspace.ResetWorkspace()
0003fcb3 op = core.CreateOperator(
0003fccd     "FC",
0003fcd7     ["X", "W", "b"],
0003fcec     ["Y"]
0003fcf9 // Create X: MxK
0003fd0a data = np.array([1,2,3,4,5,6]).astype(np.float32)
0003fd3c data = data[np.newaxis,:]
0003fd57 // Create W: NxK
0003fd68 weights = np.array(np.array([1,1/2.,1/3.,1/4.,1/5.,1/6.])).astype(np.float32)
0003fdb6 weights = weights[np.newaxis,:]
0003fdd7 // Create b: N
0003fde6 bias = np.array([1.]).astype(np.float32)
0003fe10 // Put the inputs into the workspace
0003fe35 workspace.FeedBlob("X", data)
0003fe53 workspace.FeedBlob("W", weights)
0003fe74 workspace.FeedBlob("b", bias)
0003fe93 // Run the operator
0003fea7 workspace.RunOperatorOnce(op)
0003fec5 print("Y:\n", workspace.FetchBlob("Y"))
0003fef3 **Result**
0003ff07  [[7.]]
0003ff15 </details>

0004118c This op fills an output tensor with values sampled from a uniform distribution with the range determined by the desired shape of the output. Rather, than specifying the range of values manually, the novelty of Xavier Fill is that it automatically scales the range of the distribution it draws from based on the size of the desired output tensor. For more information check out the paper [Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks](http://proceedings.mlr.press/v9/glorot10a/glorot10a.pdf). The output tensor shape is specified by the *shape* argument. However, if *input_as_shape* is set to *true*, then the *input* should be a 1D tensor containing the desired output shape (the dimensions specified in *extra_shape* will also be appended). In this case, the *shape* argument should **not** be set.
000414cb *Note: Do not set the shape argument and pass in an input at the same time.*

00043a47 The *PRelu* op takes input data tensor $X$, an input slope tensor $slope$, and produces one output tensor $Y$ of the same shape as $X.$ The op performs the element wise *PRelu* operation, defined as

00044b99 Applies the Softmax function to an n-dimensional input Tensor rescaling them so
00044be9 that the elements of the n-dimensional output Tensor lie in the range (0,1) and
00044c39 sum to 1. The softmax operator is typically the last layer in a classifier network,
00044c8d as its output can be interpreted as confidence probabilities of an input belonging
00044ce0 to each class. The input is a 2-D tensor (Tensor) of size (batch_size x
00044d28 input_feature_dimensions). The output tensor has the same shape and contains the
00044d79 softmax normalized values of the corresponding input. The softmax function is
00044dc7 defined as follows:
00044ddc $$softmax(x_i) = \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_{j} \exp(x_j)}$$
00044e15 The input does not need to explicitly be a 2D vector; rather, it will be coerced
00044e66 into one. For an arbitrary n-dimensional tensor `X` in
00044e9d $[a_0, a_1, ..., a_{k-1}, a_k, ..., a_{n-1}]$, where k is the `axis` provided,
00044eec then `X` will be coerced into a 2-dimensional tensor with dimensions
00044f31 $[(a_0 * ... * a_{k-1}), (a_k * ... * a_{n-1})]$. For the default case where
00044f7e `axis`=1, the `X` tensor will be coerced into a 2D tensor of dimensions
00044fc6 $[a_0, (a_1 * ... * a_{n-1})]$, where $a_0$ is often the batch size. In this
00045013 situation, we must have $a_0 = N$ and $a_1 * ... * a_{n-1} = D$. Each of these
00045062 dimensions must be matched correctly, or else the operator will throw errors.
000450b1 Github Links:
000450c0 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/caffe2/operators/softmax_op.h
0004510d - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/caffe2/operators/softmax_op.cc
0004515d <details>
00045168 <summary> <b>Example</b> </summary>

000451d1     "Softmax",

0004523a print("input:", workspace.FetchBlob("X"))

000452b4 **Result**

005cc5ec NSt6__ndk110__function6__baseIFvRN6caffe28OpSchemaEEEE
005cc624 The Conv2D operator computes a 2D convolution operation over an input blob $(X)$, with a filter blob $(filter)$ and a bias blob $(bias)$, and outputs a single output blob $(Y)$. Although there are several options for order, the convention is that the input $(X)$ is a blob of shape $(N,C_{in},H_{in},W_{in})$ and the output $(Y)$ is a blob of shape $(N,C_{out},H_{out},W_{out})$. Here, $N$ is the batch size, $C$ is the number of channels, $H$ is the spatial height, and $W$ is the spatial width. For example, if your input data was a batch of five, 100x120pixel RGB images, $X$ would have shape $(5,3,120,100)$.
005cc88a The $filter$ input blob may contain multiple filters and has shape $(M, C_{in}, K_H, K_W)$. Here, $M$ is the number of individual filters contained in the blob, $C_{in}$ is the number of channels of each filter (by convention in 2D convolution it is the same as the number of channels in the input), $K_H$ is the spatial height of the kernel, and $K_W$ is the spatial width of the kernel. The $bias$ blob is a vector of length $M$, where there is one bias for each filter in the $filter$ blob.
005cca79 Given the shape of the input blob and the filter blob, we can calculate the shape of the output blob as follows. The number of items in the batch $N$ will stay the same. The number of channels in the output will equal the number of kernels in the filter blob, so $C_{out} = M.$ With stride and pad defined below, the spatial height and width of the output ($H_{out}$ and $W_{out}$) are calculated as
005ccc0a $$H_{out} = \left \lfloor{\frac{H_{in} - K_H + 2*pad}{stride}+1}\right \rfloor$$
005ccc5d $$W_{out} = \left \lfloor{\frac{W_{in} - K_W + 2*pad}{stride}+1}\right \rfloor$$

005ccd54 - https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/caffe2/operators/conv_pool_op_base.h

005cf3a1 NSt6__ndk110__function6__funcIZN6caffe223AveragePoolDocGeneratorEPKcE3$_0NS_9allocatorIS5_EEFvRNS2_8OpSchemaEEEE
005cf413 consumes an input blob and applies average pooling across the blob according
005cf460 to kernel sizes, stride sizes, pad lengths and dilation. Average pooling consists
005cf4b2 of taking the average value of a subset of the input tensor according to the kernel
005cf506 size and downsampling the data into the output blob for further processing. The
005cf556 `brew` module has a wrapper for this operator for use in a `ModelHelper` object.
005cf5a8 Pooling layers reduce the spatial dimensionality of the input blob. Each of the
005cf5f8 output blob's dimensions will reduce according to:
005cf62c $$dim_{out}=\frac{dim_{in}-kernel+2*pad}{stride}+1$$
